title: Original Sin
hook: Is every baby born stamped 'Destination: Hell' because of Adam's sin?
tldr: No. Original Sin, inherited guilt deserving hellfire, came from Augustine's reading of a faulty Latin translation of Romans 5:12. The Hebrew Bible never teaches inherited guilt. Scripture teaches a human inclination toward evil: we are guilty because we sin, not because Adam did.
big_idea: You are not guilty of Adam's sin; you are guilty because you sin.

points.title: Built on a mistranslation
points.text: Augustine read Romans 5:12 in a faulty Latin version, 'in whom all sinned' instead of 'because all sinned', and concluded all humanity sinned in Adam and inherited his guilt.

points.title: Ethically unjust
points.text: Original Sin punishes all for one man's act, condemns infants, adds eternal torment to Genesis's earthly consequences, and judges limited creatures by perfect standards. Ezekiel says the son shall not suffer for the father's iniquity.

points.title: Inclination, not inherited guilt
points.text: The Bible teaches a human inclination toward evil, Yetzer Hara. Our God-given desires are not sinful; sin is born when desire is not controlled, exactly as with Eve.

points.title: Psalm 51:5 is about David
points.text: Hebrew poetry, not a doctrinal manual. Read with the KJV and Jewish tradition, 'in sin did my mother conceive me' describes the scandalous circumstances of David's own conception.

points.title: The heart can deceive, not inherently evil
points.text: Jeremiah 17:9's 'deceitful' (aqob) means cunning, untrustworthy. The heart can follow misguided emotions, but God rewards according to deeds, implying moral agency and real good.

points.title: Romans 5 cuts both ways
points.text: If Adam's disobedience made the many sinners, Christ's obedience makes the many righteous. Paul contrasts Adam and Christ to show universal sin and universal redemption.

sections.summary: Augustine of Hippo was likely the first to systematize the idea that flawed humans merit eternal hellfire, later embraced by Anselm and the Reformers, notably Calvin. ECT logic runs: Original Sin and Total Depravity make all inherit Adam's guilt and deserve endless torment; and a holy God hates sin, cannot look at sinners, and must separate and punish them eternally. 'Destination: Hell' is metaphorically stamped on every forehead, since, per John MacArthur, God only accepts absolute perfection.

Original Sin says Adam and Eve's transgression left humanity with permanent guilt and a totally depraved nature from birth, so all are condemned to hellfire by default. Calvin wrote that our nature is utterly devoid of goodness and endlessly prolific in evil. The teaching became fundamental in Reformed, fundamentalist and evangelical theology; The Gospel Coalition says because of Adam's sin we are all guilty and deserve eternal punishment.

Augustine was trying to justify infant baptism. As Ken Wilson notes, since infants have no personal sin, Augustine deduced their baptism for forgiveness must rest on guilt (reatus) inherited from Adam. His reading of Romans 5:12 relied on a faulty early Latin translation that rendered 'because all sinned' as 'in whom all sinned', implying all sinned in Adam. Inherited guilt became a cornerstone of Catholic and Protestant theology, with four ethical problems.

Condemning all humanity for one man's sin is fundamentally unjust and violates individual responsibility, central to moral and legal systems. The Old Testament stresses personal responsibility: 'The soul who sins shall die. The son shall not suffer for the iniquity of the father' (Ezekiel 18:20). Original Sin also condemns those who cannot consciously sin, such as infants, the unborn and people with severe mental impairments, contradicting a just and merciful God.

sections.h: 2. Adding on top of God's punishment
sections.summary: Adding eternal conscious torment worsens the unfairness. Genesis names only earthly consequences (Genesis 3:16-19): physical death because the Tree of Life became unavailable (Genesis 3:22) and physical suffering such as pain in childbearing, not eternal torture. Augustine's reading introduces a new, extreme and morally problematic punishment the biblical narrative does not explicitly support.

Unlike their omniscient Creator, humans are limited in wisdom, knowledge, understanding and moral decision-making, and these limits feed our propensity to sin. Misinformation, emotional stress and tiredness lead to bad decisions. Naivety and emotion made us vulnerable to temptation in Genesis 3; fatigue and illness affect the brain. Judging by perfect standards would fit only if we were made perfect like God. Our limits call for grace, not condemnation from birth.

If creation was perfect, how could Adam and Eve sin without a sinful nature, which supposedly appeared only after their first transgression? And if they could sin without a sinful nature, why is Original Sin needed to explain why people sin today?

The Bible teaches not Original Sin but a human inclination toward evil. James says each person is tempted by his own desire, and desire conceived gives birth to sin (James 1:14-15). Our flesh (sarx) has desires for security, food, water, sleep and sex. These God-given desires are not sinful; sin comes when we fail to control them by God's will. Eve saw the fruit was desirable, took it and ate, the same way we sin today.

A January 2006 DesiringGod article, 'What Is the Biblical Evidence for Original Sin?', opens by claiming Psalm 51:5 says we all come into the world as sinners. But Psalm 51 is a penitential psalm David wrote after the prophet Nathan confronted him over his adultery with Bathsheba and his arranging the death of her husband Uriah: a plea for mercy, cleansing, confession, repentance and restoration.

Reading Original Sin or Total Depravity into Psalm 51:5 is classic eisegesis: injecting one's own presuppositions into a text; the word means 'to lead into'. The passage is Hebrew poetry, full of bold, imaginative figures of speech and freedom of expression. Lifting poetic lines and using them literally as a basis for doctrine is a significant error.

In context, the verse suggests David was born into a sinful environment; only a Calvinistic translation makes it about Original Sin. The NIV reads 'Surely I was sinful at birth', an inherent moral state matching the Augustinian-Calvinist view. The mostly neutral KJV reads 'I was shapen in iniquity; and in sin did my mother conceive me', describing the circumstances of his conception. The Hebrew aligns more closely with the KJV.

David was an outcast in his family, strained with his brothers (1 Samuel 17:28) and apparently his parents: 'Though my father and mother forsake me, the LORD will receive me' (Psalm 27:10). When Samuel came to anoint one of Jesse's sons (1 Samuel 16), Jesse invited every son except David, so Samuel asked, 'Are these all the sons you have?' Only at Samuel's insistence was David sent for. How humiliating. But why was he rejected?

New Testament authors sometimes cite non-canonical, mostly Jewish, sources: Jude quotes a prophecy from the Book of Enoch (Jude 1:14-15), Paul quotes Aratus's poem Phainomena (Acts 17:28), and Jesus quotes an unknown Jewish tradition (Matthew 5:43). Historical context, including rabbinic literature, often adds insight not spelled out in the Bible.

sections.h: Conception in sin: the Talmud's story
sections.summary: The Talmud says Jesse doubted his lineage because he descended from Ruth the Moabitess (Ruth 4:17), so after seven sons he left his wife Nitzevet and planned to father children with his Canaanite maidservant. Pitying Nitzevet, the maidservant secretly switched places with her, like Leah and Rachel's deception of Jacob. Nitzevet conceived David, her eighth son, but never revealed the switch, so she was scorned as immoral and David ostracized.

Psalm 51:5 speaks to David's personal circumstances, not a doctrine that arose about 1,400 years later. 'Shapen in iniquity' and 'in sin did my mother conceive me' most likely refer to the sinful way his parents conceived him, which also explains his rejection. His rise from overlooked shepherd boy to revered king is a story of redemption and transformation through divine favor, not total depravity or original sin.

While serving at a Baptist-Calvinist ministry in Israel, the writer asked a theology professor about self-sacrificial deeds of non-Christian Jews, some who gave their lives to protect others. Citing Jeremiah 17:9-10, the professor called them selfish, seeking attention and honor. People can do evil without being inherently evil; God's image still yields much good. R.C. Sproul and John Piper read the verse as saying all are born with a deceitful, God-opposing heart.

In the Hebrew Bible the heart is the seat of will and intention, not a statement about inherent evil. Read literally, 'desperately sick' would mean heart disease; metaphorically, the heart can be swayed by evil motives but changed, as calls for a circumcised heart show (Deuteronomy 30:6). 'Deceitful' is aqob, cunning or untrustworthy, from aqab, heel, implying following or tailing: hearts follow emotions that can mislead.

sections.h: God sees motives and rewards deeds
sections.summary: Good-looking acts can hide impure, hypocritical motives (Matthew 6:5), like filming gifts to the poor for social media. God knows every motive. The verse stresses the heart's capacity for deception, not inherent evil. And it implies moral agency: God gives 'every man according to his ways, according to the fruit of his deeds', so people can do good and are responsible; otherwise why reward deeds?

Jeremiah spoke to a specific group at a specific time, possibly about Israel's moral condition then; elsewhere Israel is said to have a good heart (1 Samuel 12:20; 2 Chronicles 19:9; 1 Samuel 13:14). Reading it as universal evil ignores free will, repentance, transformation and good even in non-Christians (Acts 10:2). It describes the heart's inclination to evil, in Jewish theology the Yetzer Hara, from 'the inclination of the human heart is evil from youth' (Genesis 8:21).

sections.h: No Original Sin in the Old Testament
sections.summary: Apart from two verses taken out of context, the Old Testament conspicuously lacks Augustine's Original Sin. If foundational, it would be clear throughout the Hebrew Scriptures, especially the Law. Outside Genesis, Adam appears only twice: in a genealogy (1 Chronicles 1:1) and as an analogy for Israel's covenant breaking (Hosea 6:7). Genesis 3 describes disobedience and loss of the Tree of Life, but no transmission of guilt to humanity.

DesiringGod cites Romans 5:12 and 5:19 to say Adam's act constituted all of us sinners. But it quoted only the first half of 5:19 and omitted the crucial second half: 'so also through the obedience of the one man the many will be made righteous.' If Adam's act condemns all beforehand, Christ's makes all righteous. Paul presents Adam as a type of Christ, contrasting sin and redemption, and never says Adam's guilt is inherited.

sections.h: The Greek of Romans 5:12 and Peter Enns
sections.summary: The Greek phrase for 'because all sinned' can mean 'because' or 'in that'; none of the readings clearly support inherited guilt. Professor Peter Enns writes that the doctrine of the Fall depends absolutely on this one passage filtered through Augustine, who, from a poor Latin translation, read 'in him' where the Greek has 'because', making all humanity culpable with Adam. Neither Romans, Genesis nor the Old Testament supports it.

We live in a faulty, dying world and add our own brokenness. William Lane Craig calls Adam the floodgate through which sin entered and spread. Paul stresses universal sin and the need for global redemption, not inherited guilt. You are guilty because you sin, not for Adam's sin. Imperfect parents and world shape us, so we and our children sin, like an incurable pandemic. Even death serves a purpose: we do not suffer indefinitely.

mythfact.myth: Romans 5:12 says all humanity sinned in Adam.
mythfact.fact: That reading comes from a faulty Latin translation Augustine used. The Greek says death spread to all because all sinned.

mythfact.myth: Psalm 51:5 teaches that every person is born sinful.
mythfact.fact: It is Hebrew poetry about David's own conception, which the Talmud describes as scandalous, explaining why his family rejected him.

mythfact.myth: Genesis says Adam's sin brought eternal torment on humanity.
mythfact.fact: Genesis names only earthly consequences: physical death through losing the Tree of Life, and suffering such as pain in childbearing.

mythfact.myth: Jeremiah 17:9 proves all human good deeds are secretly selfish.
mythfact.fact: It warns the heart can deceive, but God rewards according to deeds, implying people can do real good and are responsible.

quiz.q: What did Augustine's Latin Bible wrongly say in Romans 5:12?
quiz.why: The Greek reads 'because all sinned'; the faulty Latin implied all humanity sinned in Adam.

quiz.q: According to the Talmud, why was David an outcast?
options: He was the youngest and weakest
His mother was scorned over his secret conception
quiz.why: Nitzevet conceived him by switching places with Jesse's maidservant and never revealed it, so she was called immoral.

quiz.q: What does the Hebrew aqob in Jeremiah 17:9 mean?
quiz.why: From aqab, heel: the heart tends to follow emotions that can mislead, not that it is inherently evil.
